utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination-in-chief. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We left off last week talking about your report, and I'd like to again call up in e-court 1D5358, and page 259 in Serbian, page 261 in English. It will be, I think, the previous page -- or the next page in the B/C/S. And here you have a list of attachments. Can you explain the significance of the attachments to your report.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attachments are defined, like in every monograph, every study, so as to include important information or to substantiate with arguments the information given in the body of the text. The attachments are provided mainly in the form of schematics, charts, maps, plans, et cetera. I think they carry some information which is not expressed in the body of the text, or they make it more precise and clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could turn briefly to 1D5359 in e-court. I think we see the same list before us. And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Ivetic, that we have this document in e-court twice. I don't know whether it's the same or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't either. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar has opened the first version of it. Could you please try to find out what happened during the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honours. We will. And, if we could, for the time being, just look at pages 2,3 and 4, in sequence, of the original and I guess, the translation. If the version that's been opened has those pages. Now I don't know whether what's been opened has those pages or not. It appears that it does. Here's page 2 before us on the screen, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are these the attachments that we were just discussing previously?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of the attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I had just a quick opportunity to compare the two different uploads. I do see there's a difference in the number of pages in the uploads in the B/C/S versions. I just want to note that it appears that both versions, I cannot locate specifically attachment 5 and I'm not sure that if all attachments are uploaded. If they are not, could that please happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They are not all uploaded. Some of the maps are too big to ho into e-court. So we're trying to get those copied and that's why we're not going to tender this at this time, since we still have to provide the large map to the Prosecution and find a way to get it reproduced so as to be able to introduce it with the rest of the attachments. We should be getting the original in a day or so to be able to try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then hear from you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, it doesn't like the two schematics on the screen are the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's why I asked for pages 2 and 3. I think the schematic continues on the next page in English even if the lines do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, what we have before us is a sketch of the HVO. I want to ask you a general question, sir, in relation to the VRS, the ABiH and the HVO armies, what -- how would you describe them in a military sense? What kind of army type best describes these armies?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In several places in my report, I emphasise that in Bosnia-Herzegovina the war was a traditional civil war in terms of all the elements that characterise a civil war. That in such a form of conflict of national interests of the constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslim, Serbs, and Croats, armed formations were gradually built. These armies have all the characteristics of territorial, militia-type armies, created and built up during the war and the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Considering that I've given a lot of information in my report, I don't want to go into detail and waste time, but these are basically militia-type armies. Armies that are territorial in character.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of the chronology of the formation of these three armies, the HVO, ABiH, and the VRS, what was the chronology of which was -- what was formed when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we have a clear record, if the witness could break it down by individual formation or army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, would it be a good idea to take them one by one? But if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's your witness and sometimes chronology may cover several ones. I leave it in your hands how to proceed. You're now aware of what Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let do it this way then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, in relation to the HVO, in relation to the other two army, the VRS and the ABiH, when was it formed? Chronologically.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginnings of the establishment of the HVO date back to the period when the Croatian army entered the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of Bosnian Posavina and western Herzegovina; mainly western Herzegovina where paramilitary units of the HOS were still active. The Croatian Defence Council was established and built up using all the logistics of the Croatian army from the time when the Croatian army was clashing with the JNA in the area of western Herzegovina and, after that, in the area of Kupres. As for the BH army, the roots, the beginnings of the BH army were described in the decisions of the political movement, SDA, the Party for Democratic Actions, and continued to be developed from May 1991 after the formation of the Patriotic League; that is to say, the beginning of the civil war, and the Patriotic League directed all its decisions at providing the material, the ideological and every other basis for the future arming, using resources seized from the JNA and taken from one part of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In terms of its concept and political options, the Croatian and Serbian people differed in their attitude towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. They sought and there strove to preserve nationally compact territories of their own, whereas the Party of Democratic Action, in its strategic concept, saw a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, one state without any territorial divisions dominated by a Muslim majority. For that reason, the Army of Republika Srpska was created last because they had the feeling that Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain as a whole in a so-called rump Yugoslavia, a smaller Yugoslavia. After the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina and especially after the decision of the Presidency of the former SFRY, they understood that their strategic objective to remain in the rump Yugoslavia was inachievable [as interpreted]. That's when the Territorial Defence of the Serbian people was created in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then by decision of the assembly on 12th May, the Army of Republika Srpska was also established. After the withdrawal of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army from Bosnia, room was created for the clashes between these three national armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd to call up again your report, 1D5358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While that comes up, may I ask a follow-up question. Mr. Kovac, you talked about the HVO but without any time-frame. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did mention that it was the entry of Croatian units in the area of western Herzegovina and Bosnian Posavina. In Bosnian Posavina, that happened even before the clashes in Sarajevo, in the first half of April 1992; whereas, in western Herzegovina that period began much earlier, some eight months earlier, in May and June 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 6 in both versions of the report, both languages, I'd like to look at part of paragraph 10 with you, and it is the -- starts in the middle of the last line in the bottom of the page in English and it says: "It is important to note that it was not an international conflict, nor was it ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we have to turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... any kind of aggression on BH by Yugoslavia. In question was a classical civil war of a religious and ethnic character with a significant participation of the Croatian army in parts of BH throughout the course of the war." Now, you have already again today mentioned a classical civil war. Militarily speaking, what are the characteristics or attributes of a war that is a classical civil war?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Militarily speaking, the main features of a civil war are determined by political dimensions; namely, the political aims of the conflicting parties in any state. On that basis, strategic objectives are defined. On that basis, armed formations are defined. And all the other elements are built up during the war. In this paragraph, it is precisely stated that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not a war between states. No armed forces from outside came to that war from outside except the Croatian forces in a particular period that are mentioned. Other features of a civil war are that there is not enough professional personnel in armed formations, and the fate of the people is closely attached to armed units. Whenever armed units move, they are followed by the people. Also, from experience and from research into wars even before Bosnia-Herzegovina, another feature is that it's impossible to completely exercise will from the strategic to the tactical level because there are a multitude of armed units that are difficult to place under command control, and the civilian population of the warring parties suffer. And population is frequently moved to territories controlled by one's own armed units. I could go on, but these are the main characteristics of a civil war, national or religious. I also emphasised that in this war the religious conflict between the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina was prominent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That was going to be my next question. In relation to the religious aspect of the war, if we can take a look at paragraph 12 of your report and we have to go on the next page in the Serbian to do that. And in this paragraph, in the second part of the paragraph, you mention a text called "The Islamic Declaration," authored by Alija Izetbegovic and it is mentioned multiple times in your report. I would first like to ask: How was that book received when it was published in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me note that Alija Izetbegovic during his life expressed determinations of that type in his ties with the organisation of Young Muslims, and that means extremist activity and organisation of the state based on political Islam. "The Islamic Declaration" in that context is a platform for organising and structuring Bosnia-Herzegovina as a unitarian state dominated by the Muslim people, with relations between people and a system of values that is not close to the Croatian and Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One can say that "The Islamic Declaration" was met by Serbs and Croats as a threat; that is, creating a basis for conflict between peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And from 1990, the Muslim people in their majority was accepted -- the Muslim people accepted it as a basis for their organisation and for the creation of the Green Berets and, later, their own army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to highlight a few portions of that book to ask you some questions. So if we could please call up in e-court D557 MNA, and we'll need the bottom of page 29 in the English and page 22 in Serbian, the second paragraph from the top. And, here, sir, the text in the English says: "First and foremost of these conclusions is certainly the incompatibility of Islam with non-Islamic systems. There can be neither peace nor co-existence between the Islamic religion and non-Islamic social and political institutions. The failure of these institutions to function and the instability of the regimes in Muslim countries manifest in frequent change and coup d'etat is most often the consequence of their a priori opposition to Islam, as the fundamental and foremost feeling of the peoples in these countries. But claiming the right to order its own world itself, Islam obviously excludes the right or possibility of action on the part of any foreign idealogy on that terrain. There is it, therefore, no lay principle, and the state should both reflect and support religious moral concepts." Sir, militarily speaking, how do you interpret this first selection that we've read from "The Islamic Declaration" of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I talked about political Islam. I thought that this concept contains within itself all these things quoted here and political Islam implies a system of values and an organisation of social relations based on Islam and exclusivity vis-à-vis other peoples and faiths and their exclusion from state administration and government. This excerpt that you quoted says, generally speaking, that these positions are an operalisation [as interpreted] of political Islam and they reflect the attitude of Alija Izetbegovic and the top leadership of the party towards organising the future state as uniatic [as interpreted] and Islamic. It is that attitude that was the trigger for the resistance of the other two constituent people in terms of how the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised. I can comment in detail on each of these concepts, but I believe the basic idea is reflected in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to just highlight one more part of this book by going to page 55 in the English and it will be the second paragraph under "Islamic governance" and it will be page 43 in the Serbian in the middle of the page. And it reads as follows: "We must therefore be, first, preachers and then soldiers. Our weapons are personal example, the book and word. When is force to be joined to these? The choice of this moment is always a tangible one, and depends on a series of factors. There is, however, a general rule. The Islamic movement should and can start to take over power as soon as it is morally and numerically strong enough to be able to overturn not only the existing non-Islamic government, but also to build up a new Islamic one. This differentiation is important." Sir, militarily speaking, what do these words in "The Islamic Declaration," what are they calling for, what kind of action?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically without going into any detailed descriptions, this kind of concept and conclusions means that armed formations should be established and that they would create a new Islamic government and a new Islamic state, according to the wishes and will of a Islamic political system. That is the basis of "The Islamic Declaration." That is the core of "The Islamic Declaration" as a platform for activity in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I expressed that a moment ago when I spoke about the Patriotic League and the Green Berets that were paramilitary formations that preceded the establishment of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Defence would tender D557 MNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this exhibit was last discussed, I believe, on the 22nd of January 2015 at transcript page 30443. At that time the Defence had tried to tender this 77-page declaration and the Chamber had requested submissions from the Defence as to why the whole portions are relevant. I believe that we're in the same position. If the Defence would like to file those submissions, we're willing to accordingly respond to them. On the last time that it came up, the Chamber had set a deadline and there were no submissions that had been received by the Defence, so the Trial Chamber denied the admission of D557 without prejudice at the time. So I believe it's a renewed situation where we should now get those submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this instant moment, this is a text that has been cited multiple times in the expert report of the witness we have before us, who has now given us evidence of how the words in "The Islamic Declaration" were received and what effect they had on the events that transpired. Therefore, I think it is necessary to have a full picture of the context of these words and the text that was published in 1990 that is being cited in the expert report of this witness, which is why I have renewed the request of the Defence to have this introduced into evidence at this time, since I believe it arises from the expertise of the witness and is an important document to have in the record so that we can understand the evidence of this witness in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I see in footnote 6 that as a general reference to the whole of "The Islamic Declaration" is the -- therefore, it's not very specific. So you are saying that the witness refers to it but -- and he does, but I've got no idea whether that refers to all of the 77 pages or whether there are special portions. For example, I see on our screen at this moment something about Pakistan. I don't know whether he refers to that in this context as well, how relevant that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, on the basis of what you said the Chamber is not yet convinced that the whole of "The Islamic Declaration" should be admitted into evidence. You've read a specific portion, I think, even two specific portions. There's no problem in admitting that into evidence but if you want more than the portions you specifically dealt with, then the Chamber invites you again to make submissions as why the rest is needed and then specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are guided by your decision and will then do. So I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile at this moment, only 77 pages are uploaded so the portions I think you dealt with, you read them into the record, so even there might not be a need to have those pages in evidence, but we wait for your further submissions and at this moment -- May I take it that what you just told us at this moment is that you, at this moment, withdraw your renewed application for -- or tendering of the whole of the document and that we'll hear from you what portions you'd like. Or if you insist on the whole of it, that we learn from your submissions why it is that we should admit that or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The second of the options that Your Honour has listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we leave it for the time being. The status remains as it was before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could return to the expert of General Kovac. That is 1D5358. And page 8 in both languages and paragraph number 17. And paragraph 17 begins on the bottom of the page in English and bleeds over to the next page and most of paragraph 17 is on this page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But here you talk of the actions of the SDA as to the creation of the Patriotic League and as to its activities in relation to the JNA. When did all these activities begin in relation to the release of the book that we just looked at, "The Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in 1991, in May, activities started, aimed at implementing "The Islamic Declaration" with the view to the Islamicisation of society and the establishment of paramilitary formations. The basic task of the SDA was carried out by Lieutenant-Colonel Sefer Halilovic, who had deserted from the JNA, and together with a number of associates, he worked on the organisation of staffs of the Patriotic League throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily in municipalities where the Muslim population was the majority population. The extremist part of the Patriotic League were the members of the Green Berets. They were a better trained formation for carrying out these tasks in the initial period of the conflict with the units of the JNA. And in terms of taking over materiel and other equipment from depots and barracks of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. The Patriotic League, throughout this period, from May until April; that is to say, May 1991 until April 1992, so it's almost a year, they held several meetings that have been accentuated in this report. There was a constant ascent in terms of organisation and as the crisis was coming to a head, units of the Patriotic League were being established either within Territorial Defence units in municipalities with a majority Muslim population -- well, in conclusion, one can say that "The Islamic Declaration" was a political platform for the military organisation of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. For transmitting these positions to the people and in order to win over the members of these organisations from a moral point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How did the Patriotic League compare in size to the peace-time JNA army?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As JNA units were withdrawing from Slovenia and later on Croatia, were becoming so different. They were basically on paper only. They did not have real combat power because, inter alia, members of the Muslim people had deserted from these units as the civil war was getting closer. As the Patriotic League was getting stronger, and you can see from these documents the hostile attitude taken towards the JNA and the blockade of the places where JNA troops were staying and also making it impossible for them to move freely through Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as the crisis developed, they were taking over part of the weapons of the JNA and materiel wherever they could. The JNA was getting weaker and weaker from a moral and personnel and any other point of view. We had this situation that at the very beginning of the civil war, that is to say, the 6th of April, the Patriotic League had about 120.000 members and there were about 103 municipal staffs and a series of units at brigade and detachment level. They are specifically listed in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did the then-existing military laws allow for the creation of such a privately armed group by a political party?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All laws and regulations starting with the constitution and the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army did not allow the creation of paramilitary formations. However, unfortunately -- however, unfortunately - may I continue now? - it was the reality of civil war itself that brought the conflict parties into a situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were supposed to set up units in order to protect themselves from this unitary concept of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to take look at another document, Exhibit D412, and this is referenced in paragraphs 1.97 and 2.7 of your report. And while we wait for that document to come up on the screen -- and we see that it is dated the ... 29th of April, 1992. And if we could -- it says it's from the Territorial Defence Staff. If we could look at the next page with the signature. I guess the ... this is the original without the signature. Could you tell us, based upon the structure that is sending this document -- if we can go to the first page in English, so we can follow along in English as well, where it is the staff of the Territorial Defence in the Ministry for National Defence of the Republic of BiH, what can you tell us about this structure that is sending out this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial Defence Staffs of republics of the former SFRY did not have the right to use units of the TO - or Territorial Defence, let me give the full name - without decisions taken by the Supreme Command or the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In that sense, this document, in this period, is, in essence, unlawful in relation to the regulations of the joint state that was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. As for the content of the document itself, basically it expresses aggression, an aggressive attitude towards the units of the JNA along the lines of blockade, preventing them from moving about freely, taking over their weaponry, equipment, materiel, and carrying out combat operations vis-à-vis the structures of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to take a look at 65 ter number 31023 in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before that comes up, can -- Mr. Kovac, can you tell me what is written in handwriting on top of the page? You see in B/C/S at the moment. Oh, thank you. It was missing. I couldn't see it in the English. Now it's clear. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter number 31023. And I think we'll see it is dated also the 29th of April, 1992 from the Ministry of Interior, and we see at the bottom of the B/C/S the name of Alija Delimustafic, which I think is on the next page in English, but let's stay with this page for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you: How do the activities that are being ordered by Mr. Delimustafic in this document compare with the one we just looked at; and what conclusions do you draw from the same?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to proceed from the fact that at that time this was not the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We see that this document also invokes a decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In essence, this was not a joint government of all three peoples. This was the government of the Muslim people, and that can explicitly be seen through this document of Delimustafic's. This order is based on that decision of the Presidency or, rather, Alija Izetbegovic, and the decision of the republic staff of the Territorial Defence. We also see in terms of the content of these paragraphs in the order, this just means spelling out in more precise terms the same positions that are contained in the order of the territorial staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Another thing: We see here that the units of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already become units of the Muslim people only in the area that was under the control of Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 31023 receives exhibit number D1355, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to talk more about this concept of the Territorial Defence by first looking at your report, 1D5358, and page 29 in the English, page 28 in the Serbian, and I think it's paragraph 1.57 and onwards where you talk about the Territorial Defence, but I'd like to look at paragraph 1.58 with you. In this paragraph, you describe that the JNA was the core of the Yugoslav armed forces under the 1982 Law of ONO. Was the Territorial Defence part of or separate from the JNA under this law?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of all republics was an integral part of the armed forces of the SFRY, the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In no way could these units be considered as separate armed units. They were part of a single system of command and control over the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the JNA, did the command of the JNA command over the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top of the strategic level of command there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I guess it's okay. I might have prematurely gotten up because I guess we're talking about a doctrinal level. However it goes into a factual level I believe there has already been discussion of different types of territorial defences in different time periods, if we could have greater specificity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you were on your feet I interrupted the witness, and please try to avoid be prematurely on your feet so that the witness can finish his answer. Witness, I interrupted you for the reason I just explained. Could you please resume your answer. I leave it to you, Mr. Ivetic, whether you want to repeat the question either in exactly the same way or in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to the Territorial Defence under the 1982 Law on ONO, in relation to the JNA, did the command of the JNA command over the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At strategic level, there was a single command. That was the Supreme Command. And it commanded units at operative and strategic level; that is to say, through the General Staff of the JNA. We can say that at operative and tactical level and in accordance with regulations, it was defined that in the zone in which armed forces are being used, the protagonist, in terms of the unification of all the forces, is the command of the JNA, from strategic to tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And Territorial Defence units under the SFRY, were they trained to be -- what kind of units were they trained to be?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the concept of All People's Defence and social self-protection, the units of the Territorial Defence are conceived as units of a structure that would defend a particular zone, area in terms of acting together; that is to say, JNA units and TO units. So their aim is to operationalise the concept of All People's Defence, to make it possible for the largest number possible of soldiers to take part in defence from external aggression. This concept is based on the position of the then-Yugoslavia that was not a member of any military alliance, namely neither of the Warsaw Pact or NATO. And it had to be capable of defending itself. The second basis for this organisation is the socialisation of the function of defence in the then-system of socialist self-management. Or rather, getting the function of defence as close as possible to each and every citizen, making it possible for these citizens to take part in defence against external aggression. However, unfortunately, this state had overlooked the possibility of civil war and breaking up the country through a civil war. In that way, and the units of the Territorial Defence were taken advantage of as a material basis for the creation of national armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One final question before the break, under the SFRY system, were Territorial Defence units foreseen as being used as manoeuvre units?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically Territorial Defence units had a space structure, aerial structure. In terms of the equipment of certain units, some of them are defined as manoeuvre units of the Territorial Defence; namely, that they could move from one area or space to another within the republic or within the combat zone, but that is a smaller number. Basically their structure was one based on area. That is to say, that they were manned by people from that particular area in order to carry out tasks within that local area. That is to say, the municipality, the local commune, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Witness, we take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at paragraph 1.71 of your report found on page 32 in English, 31 in the Serbian. In this paragraph, you talk about the mistrust of JNA officers of the TO. And then in the next paragraph, 1.72, which starts on the bottom of the page in the Serbian and goes onto the next page, you talk about the reorganisation of the entire system in 1986 under the plan Jedinstvo. What was the objective of this 1986 reorganisation.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts are presented in this report to say that in this period from the death of Josip Broz, national tensions sporadically were rising in the former Yugoslavia, and the estimate was that it was possible to expect the abuse of some Territorial Defence units and utilize them unlawfully. There were also many other factors that contributed to a change in the organisation of the Yugoslav People's Army, in the sense that there was a shift from the army principle to Military Districts, and in the Yugoslav theatre of war, as envisaged by the defence plan, a new model of organisation was made which, from these Military Districts, united JNA units and TO units at local level without taking into account republican borders, because they did not coincide with the military estimate of what a Yugoslav theatre of war would look like. If necessary, I can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's enough for now. I want to ask about one other specific part of this paragraph and I think we need to go onto the next page in the Serbian in order to discuss that. In talking about the Jedinstvo plan of reorganisation, you talk about the JNA taking over and being in charge of storing TO weapons and ammunition in its depots. Under the SFRY system, what kind of weapons and weapons systems was the Territorial Defence equipped with?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was basically well equipped. The same as the majority of JNA units, especially in the B class, those that did not have a full complement of personnel. The Territorial Defence units in the more developed republics, such as Slovenia, had even more modern equipment, in communications, some infantry weapons, and moveable anti-aircraft defence systems. Why did these estimates get things correctly? We can see that now in hindsight the aim was to increase the security of weapons and reduce the possibility that arms may be abused at local levels by political elites which had already been growing from Communism into national organisations in the territories of republics, which were ever-more open to separatist activity and the possibility of secession from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to focus on the JNA for a bit. If we could turn to page 243 in the English and page 241 of the Serbian of your report, I propose to look at paragraph 6.8 of the same. And in this paragraph, you say: "The former JNA, and consequently all three armies in the war in BH, did not have a classical Soviet model of commanding (centralised command model), which is strictly determined by the will of the superiors, but a combined command model which resided upon unity of command and subordination and which enabled subordinates to exhibit full creativity when decisions were made and implemented." And now we have to go to the next page in the B/C/S: "This was particularly true of the war in BH in periods between major operations, when full creativity and independence was expected of decision-makers at all levels of command. After 1960, the JNA abandoned the Soviet model of command, increasingly decentralising the organisation of the armed" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now we have to go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... forces and the command function. Flexibility and creativity of subordinates in the chain of command were, in fact, a characteristic of the armies of all three warring sides. Over 70 per cent of the time in the war in BH was spent in conflicts at the lowest tactical level and exchanges of fire, actions which were decided by commanders, komandir, of squads, platoons, companies (batteries) and commanders of battalions in all three armies in BH." Now, first of all, how did the JNA come to this abandonment of the Soviet model in 1960? What were the reasons for the same?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the model of command is concerned, there are basically these three classical models, not only the centralised and decentralised but also the combined one. But that is more in theory. In terms of doctrine, each of them has its own features determined not by individual states and armies but each state and army can be discussed separately as to the way they used the army. As for Yugoslavia after the Second World War and before the war, it had this centralised model, but as all functions were becoming more socialised, so did -- so was the defence system. There was a prominent need to decentralise the system of command, but not as far as decentralising it. Instead, it developed into a combined model of command. This combined model of command was improved after the constitutional changes in 1974, by giving more independence and more powers to republics; also in the functions of defence and in forming TO units. Through combat rules, through textbooks, and also "The Strategy of Armed Struggle," which was the basic doctrine document in the JNA, one can see a clear option, a clear choice of the combined model of command which is legally formulated in the basic combat documents beginning with the combat rules of the employment of units, up to the rules that determined the work of commands and staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph you have used the term "lowest tactical level," and then earlier today you talked about strategic and operative level. Could you please define for us what are these various levels within the army.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically then during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the civil war, but also in most armies in the world, these three levels of command are basic and dominant. The strategic level means the political level and the top leadership of the army; that is to say, the political/military level of command. The operative level means operative units, that is, the level of corps and operative groups. And the tactical level is from brigade commands downwards. All tactical groups that were formed as temporary units, and within itself it contained several tactical levels, such as companies, batteries and platoons, and that level was present in all the three armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like that take a look at Exhibit P2629 in e-court. Last week when you talked about Prosecution experts whom you reviewed, you mentioned General Sir Dannatt. We have, at least in the English, the statement of General Lord Dannatt. Is this one of the reports that you reviewed for purposes of your expertise in this case, the Mladic case?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I studied this report, but looking at it and drawing from my own knowledge and experience, I formulated my own report on commands in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Considering the previous level of command, that is to say, in the JNA, there are other factors that are important to the definition of the command system. That is to say, the availability of adequate command structure in militia-type armies which have few professional soldiers. It's difficult to apply the centralised model of command. And another factor is the technology the equipment and techniques. Communication systems were mostly obsolete; they consisted mainly of the assets of the former JNA and these communications systems did not make it possible to have real time communication. Superior commanders received a picture of the situation on the ground mainly through reports from lower commanders. This was very important for communication between different levels of command. We know that modern armies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the names of various communications systems in modern armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you should interrupt the witness, otherwise we will not have a proper transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, the interpreters have asked you to repeat the names of the various communications systems in modern armies that you mentioned so that had they could translate the same.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I sometimes forget myself and speed up. I'll slow down. I think I was talking about the technological factor which is very important for types or models of command. The technological factor in armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina was obsolete. Communications systems were mostly obsolete, too old, and they did not make it possible to communicate information in real time from the lowest tactical level up to the operative and later, strategic level, so that commanders at the operative level, and especially at the level of the General Staff, had delayed information. A lot of time passed before they received the reports about the situation on the ground, and for that reason, the centralised model of command could not apply. Modern armies today have developed command and information systems from tactical to strategic level under the symbolic name of C3I or C4I, that enable communication in real time, secure communication, including video images showing key areas in the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look together at page 7 in the English and page 6 in the Serbian of General Lord Dannatt's report, and paragraph 28 of the same. And he is talking about the Soviet model, the Befehlstaktik, as he calls it, the centralised command model used in conscript armies. And if we could turn the page in both versions of the report. At the end of the paragraph he says: "The fact that the armed forces of all three former warring factions in Bosnia exhibit the same inflexibility does not surprise me as the core of their military leadership is all drawn from the former JNA." And then in paragraph 30, he claims that the VRS and the JNA are both based on the Soviet, or Befehlstaktik, model of centralised command. What are your observations or conclusions about General Dannatt's description of the command style employed by both the JNA and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking a moment ago about the development of the command system in the JNA, and I emphasise again the Soviet model, after the Cominform, was abandoned militarily and otherwise, in 1964, especially after the constitutional changes in 1974 and beginning with 1980s, this model was modernised, also through new strategic and doctrine document and instructions and command and control and the combat rules of units at the level of corps and brigades. I don't think we can talk about the transfer of the centralised model of command from the JNA onto the armies involved in the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Instead, we can talk about the transfer or shift towards combined -- a combined model of command. Also, for technological reason, the obsolete equipment, the lack of sufficient professional personnel, the units and commands of both the VRS, the ABH, and the HVO transferred a lot of responsibility and independence to subordinate units, especially to the operative level, and that is the level of corps and operative groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in testifying at this trial in support of his conclusions, General Dannatt, at transcript page 19056, lines 15 to 23, suggested that Yugoslavia was a "looser member of the Warsaw Pact." Was Yugoslavia ever a member of the Warsaw Pact?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was never a member of the Warsaw Pact and Cominform is a well known event, from 1964 when there was a danger of the Warsaw Pact intervening and they built up forces preparing for an aggression against the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. From that time on, Yugoslavia received significant assistance from the west, primarily from the US, in order to rearm many branches and services in the army, beginning with its aviation and tank units, artillery, et cetera. Those weapons remained in the units of the JNA. After the Cominform, politically speaking, Yugoslavia profiled itself as a neutral and later non-aligned state, and did not belong to any political or military alliance. It had more communication and more co-operation and received more assistance from NATO than from the Warsaw Pact, but it was a non-aligned state.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now General Lord Dannatt also in supporting his conclusion that the JNA followed the Soviet model, at transcript page 19093, line 22, to 19094, line 2, claimed that this was because many officers of the JNA were sent for instruction to Russia. Do you know if the JNA ever sent officers to any other foreign nation for instruction?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with its own estimates, the JNA did send its officers for training to other countries. We can say that up to 1948 it was mostly in the Soviet Union, but after that many of those officers suffered professionally and were completely marginalised. And after the Cominform, the bulk of officers were sent to prestigious military academies in the west, but mostly they relied on their own system of training and schooling of officers. Many career officers also graduated from schools in the west, but most of them graduated from domestic academies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, also in his testimony in this case, General Dannatt, at transcript page 19107, lines 7 through 21, claimed that the VRS came from a Military District of the JNA; and then later at 19164, lines 3 through 20, he clarified that he was talking of the 2nd Military District. What can you say to about this? Is it fair or accurate to say that the VRS, in essence, was the 2nd Military District or that the Main Staff of the VRS equated to the command of that district?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite frankly, there are no facts to support this kind of assertion, and this kind of position cannot be based on the projection of personnel or materiel or the establishment of the Military District when compared to the Army of Republika Srpska. Perhaps more time would be needed to describe this entire process of withdrawing the JNA from the territory of Croatia where part of the units from that area were deployed in the area of Croatia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to some more details. But staying for a moment with the comparison between the 2nd Military District of the JNA and the command of the same and the Main Staff of the VRS, how would you compare the number of officers present in the commands of the 2nd Military District, on the one hand, and the VRS Main Staff on the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the professionals, the Military District is different from the top echelons of the organisation of an entire army. In terms of personnel, when the General Staff, say, of the Army of Republika Srpska, it wasn't properly manned so one cannot speak of similarities in terms of personnel and also officers of the Military District did not, for the most part, become officers on the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. On the contrary. Most of the officers of the 2nd Military District left together with their units after the decision was made to withdraw to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Very few officers made up the command at the level of the VRS, the Main Staff as it was called. At first, these were just tens of officers -- or, rather, ten, 15, and then only later were the elements of the organisational structure of the Main Staff built. So this kind of symmetry does not exist between the command of the Military District and the command of the Main Staff. Not in terms of structure, not in terms of personnel. Personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could return to your report, 1D5358, and if we could look at page 51 in the English, page 50 in the Serbian, and if we can look at paragraph 2.10. You have already talked a little bit about the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia. Here, in this paragraph, you say in the middle of the paragraph, line 4 at the end -- the sentence beginning on line 4 in the English: "It should be added at this point that most of the JNA assets which were in the possession of the JNA units were transferred to FR Yugoslavia during the pullout." Now when you say "most ... assets were transferred," what kind of assets are you talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about all modern, complex assets, I'm referring to all units. And primarily as regards the air force, then more modern tanks, more modern artillery equipment, and part of the logistics that have to do with maintenance institutes. Due to blockades and similar problems that we discussed a moment ago, it was hard to get all that to the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia. Also, signals equipment and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this paragraph, you also say that the other two ethnic communities seized some assets of the JNA. How did the removal, on the one hand, of most assets to Yugoslavia and the seizure of other assets by the other two ethnic groups, how did those affect the ability of the VRS to function with similar capabilities as the 2nd Military District of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for weaponry and equipment itself, I referred to the more modern equipment that could have been exported, and if not, it was the local communities that got a hold of that because of the blockade of barracks and the impossibility to get this to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As for the Serb people, after the decision was made to have the JNA withdrawn, the Serb people were compelled to ask for weapons and take weapons the same way, from the TO. That is to say, where they were the majority population. They did that from the JNA units that were in such areas to take materiel, weapons, et cetera, as did the other two ethnic communities, the other two peoples in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, the VRS Main Staff headquarters in Han Pijesak, what was that structure foreseen to be under the old Yugoslav military system? What kind of command post was that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the days of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, that's the way infrastructure was built. This was the central zone of the Yugoslav theatre of war. It was a reserve position for the Supreme Command. From the days of the kingdom, it was improved. Work conditions were improved. And there was proper maintenance for it to be able to function. As for the theatre of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, since the Serb population is the majority population in that area, it was assessed that this position would be appropriate for the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at paragraph 2.49 of your report, found on page 62 in the English and 61 in the Serbian, here you say that the VRS was formed on 12 May 1992. But "only as of the 5 June 1992 is it possible and justified to say that the necessary prerequisites were created for commanding the military organisation at all levels in accordance with authority." Could you explain that for us, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of the fact that the decision was made to establish the Army of Republika Srpska during the commotion of civil war, it cannot be considered possible to command all units at all levels of command when at many of these command positions there weren't proper appointments yet. Who would carry out duties heading these units? This date, the 15th of June, just speaks about the fundamentals of the system of command, certainly not about a properly established hierarchy system of command that would be too simplified to say that an army could be created within a span of a single month. These are just the contours of an army and they were gradually built upon throughout the war. Many problems in terms of commands were not resolved even up until the end of the war. The situation was similar in the BH army and in the HVO. I've already said at the very start that these were militia-like people's armies without sufficient personnel in terms of officers, commissioned and non-commissioned, in relation to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And ... if we could look together at P3027 in e-court, this is dated 16 April 1992 and is from the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we were to go to the next page, I think we see it is signed by the president. This talks about the -- or, pardon me, the minister, Mr. Subotic. This talks about the formation of the Territorial Defence or TO as the armed force of the Serbian republic. In a military sense, what does this mean? How was this initial army structured?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, this was not an army yet. It has to be brought into the context of the situation prevailing in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. This was the beginning of the civil war itself, about ten days after these armed conflicts between the paramilitaries and also taking weapons from depots of the TO, the JNA, the control of ethnic territories and the protection of villages and towns based on the structure of the population. This document is a reaction to the already adopted documents by the Muslim people and the Croats. In essence, it represents the beginning of the armed organisation of the Serb people as well, because it was obvious that there would not be any other armed protection except for their own units that they would establish themselves. So, in that sense, one can say that this was the start of the Army of Republika Srpska or, rather, the organisation of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the later integration of these units organised as Territorial Defence units into the Army of Republika Srpska cause any difficulties in relation to the manner of operation of the units?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gradually some of these units were renamed; others were unified; but they, in themselves, did not constitute a problem, unless they remained at the level of paramilitary organisation. But there were some units that became renegade units, in relation to the command system of the VRS. Even up until 1993. And later on. These were smaller units that constituted a problem in terms of command, the use of units of the VRS, and especially for carrying out agreements and the like. Basically most of these TO units did become part of the structure of the VRS through a regular process, whereas, part of them were politically taken advantage of and they were actually paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D5358, your report, page 65 in the English and page 63 in the B/C/S, and look at paragraph 2.55.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're still waiting for the English, it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, here, you talk about the fact that the reserve officers accounted for most of the officer corps in the VRS and that there's a high percentage of casualties within that officer corps. What effect did the prevalence of reserve officers have on the command and control abilities of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska did not have enough personnel but they also did not have enough reserve officers. One can say that these reserve officers were not very professional because in the pre-war period for quite a while they had not been receiving training, and therefore one could not say they were prepared to carry out their duties. Basically they were soldiers too. At a higher academic level though, most of them had university degrees and with a bit more of military training, but they could not be compared to professional officers in any way. These numbers that pertained to their presence did not really resolve the problem of the lack of professional officers. Professional officers constituted a small part of the structure. Or perhaps it would be better to say the establishment of the VRS included very few professional officers, especially at tactical level. That is to say, brigades, brigade commands, to platoon level. This is precisely stated in the report. Commanders of companies and even battalions were soldiers or reserve officers at battalion level, but mostly these command duties were carried out by soldiers who came from their own settings. This shows that this was a territorial people's army of the militia type.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look very briefly at P338. This is an analysis, and I have a paper copy if it will assist you to have a paper copy since I know the text is rather tiny in e-court. This is an analysis of the Army of Republika Srpska drafted in 1993 relating to the time-period of 1992. I'd like to look at page 71 in the English and page 68 in the Serbian. And I want to look first at this table that's at the bottom of page 68 and I'd like for you to explain to us what is the difference between these categories, the first one being "envisaged war establishment strength" and in Serbian it is "[B/C/S spoken]." What is that compared to actual strength?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to war establishment; that is to say, as prescribed, as established and the manning level is what the situation actually was. If I may note, this pertains to the total number of officers, professional and reserve officers. To the best of my recollection, there were a lot less professional officers. There were about 1500, and the remainder of this figure of over 6.000 were reserve officers. So if we take into account their representation at tactical level, it goes down even to less than 5 per cent of the prescribed levels by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I think we need page 64 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because what we're looking at is not corresponding with the English version we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the headings were the same and I apologise for that. I just looked up and saw that the two did not correlate to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now looking at this table on the bottom of page 64, based upon this information, the conclusion as to the GS VRS, which I believe is the Main Staff, it says that at 51 per cent of its establishment strength if I'm reading the table correctly. First of all, am I reading the table correctly; and if so, how would that affect the functioning of the Main Staff, especially as to command and control?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Main Staff is in this first line. And that refers to the figure of 50 per cent of 122 so at the level of 51 per cent, together with all categories of personnel. As for officers, it is less than 50 per cent, about 45 per cent, as far as I can see. As for the last line, it refers to the level of the entire army. Out of the envisaged 12.961, there were only 1.332 officers. But that's at the level of the entire army. And then, if we take into account that most of -- most of these officers out of the 1.332 were at commands of operational and strategic level, then we see that there were very few professional soldiers in the units at tactical level; brigades, battalions, companies, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 51 per cent, could you explain to that -- to me again, what that now stands for? I see 51 is at the very last column, although there's no heading for it, but I think in the original B/C/S the heading says percentage. Now, what is 51 per cent a percentage of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this percentage, 51 per cent, pertains to the manning level as related to the establishment of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for all categories of personnel. Officer, non-commissioned officer, soldiers. Not only officers therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. Do I understand, then, that the -- let me see. I see that, according to establishment, the total would be 146. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All categories of personnel in the Main Staff, yes, that is to say, NCOs and soldiers included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I know that the actual war strength was 72. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were 72. But we can see here a significant lack of officers. It is significantly less than 51 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. But on the total, I have difficulties in understanding how 72 out of 146 could be 51 per cent. 50 per cent of 146 is 73. So how 72 could be more than 50 per cent is a puzzle for me. I would rather think of 49 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 146. And 90, I think, in the previous column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps my -- some of the columns are not -- but even what does the 90 stand for? I've got no idea. Because -- at least in the English translation, but I see the same is true for the original, there's no heading for that column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to all these categories of personnel, there is an empty rubric. I believe it's also a percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what we believe is -- could you now tell me what 51 per cent represent what of what? A percentage is always a number in relation to a total number. Now could you tell me what the number is and related to what total number I find 51 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As this table is drawn up, 72 is from 140 to -- I can't see the last digit well. Is it 6 or 0? I think it's 0. But that's the ratio. Now beginning with the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no. You said 72 out of 140? Where I do find the 140?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next, according to the war establishment, the fourth column in the first row. 140, and then is it 6 or 0? But in terms of percentage, it should be 0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we enlarge that so that we can see whether it's, indeed, 140 or 146. No, could we enlarge it in the original. In the English, it's clear. Yes. Seems to be, rather, 146 than a 0 at the end. But apart from that ... and then you would still say that even if it's 140, then 72 makes 51 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 146. In the English version, you can see it's a 6. And judging by the sum of these previous numbers, it's 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, therefore, 51 per cent is not accurate then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going into that part of arithmetic, sir. Arithmetically speaking, no, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, it seems to be an error --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're at the time for the next break, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are perhaps even already beyond that. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you, after the break, could you try also to clarify what the double numbers in some of the columns mean such as officers 61 and then also 59 or 50 and 94. Because that's not entirely clear. And is there any way that we could understand what the empty -- the columns without titles, what they stand for? Unless we should translate anything from the left part, but I still do not know exactly how to interpret this table. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to assist, I would just note that we've had evidence related to this table from Mr. Theunens back on 9th of December, 2013, if that assists Mr. Ivetic with -- and on the specific numbers that the Chamber just asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit that I had forgotten about that. I hope that is -- can be forgiven. We take a break, and resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, as far as timing is concerned, I think you have a little bit less than half an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've got more. I think. I'm approximately, I think, from my questions about hour and a half to two hours even depending how the speed of the answers comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you asked for three hours. You are over two and a half hours how. That's -- and I think the witness cannot be blamed for not answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Try to stick as much as you can to your original timing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because I don't see many explanations at this moment why it should be more. There was one other matter about two versions uploaded into e-court. Has that been clarified?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That has, Your Honours, there should be only one version, that is 1D5359. That is the correct version, although it is still not complete because of that issue with the maps that we mentioned earlier. And that I discussed with the Office of the Prosecution to see, once we get the original from Belgrade, how we can reproduce that in a format to get it into e-court given its size, as indeed many of the maps had difficulty of being uploaded in to the system due to the size of the scans were that generated from them. But I'm told there is now only one document in e-court bearing that 65 ter number so we've at least made it more -- easier to locate the document in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, the Trial Chamber has asked me to try to see if you can help clarify this table a little bit further. In relation to the "[B/C/S spoken]" or "actual war establishment strength," for the Main Staff, there's a number under officers of 61 and then to the right of that is a number that is 50, with that column not being labelled. What is your understanding of that figure at the top of 50 and then under 1st Krajina Corps underneath we see 59 in that same position in that unmarked column?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me again which column is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- well, we just lost the pointer. If -- there. Up a little. Up a little. Stop there. Right where the cursor is located on the Serbian version, which is the number 50, and it's the first unmarked column in the part of the table that says "actual war establishment strength." What's your understanding of what that 50 would entail?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number 50, I believe, is the percentage ratio, the number of officers, 122, and the actual strength, 61. And that is exactly 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there's a number below that, which is 94, and then in the column for officers, there's a second number as well, which is 59. Do you have any understanding or appreciation of what those figures might represent?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it in the key, nor did I deal with that second number, but that first number in the denominator is the ratio between the planned, or envisaged, and the actual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's -- under 61, we see 59. Could you explain what that 59 stands for? And we are still in the first row. And now the first column, "actual war establishment strength," under 61, we see 59. What does 59 stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's when you look at the total, the ratio between the number of professional officers and the total number of officers. You can see that in the last line, where you see that, in total, in relation to the VRS, the number of -- the number of officers is 6.000-something and the actual number of professional officers is 332. So this is the number of professional officers out of the total number of officers. So 59 were professional officers and 2 were reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what then stands the 94? What does that relate to there in the next column? You see there 50 and below it 94. What does then the 94 stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a percentage. The first number is 50 per cent. It means that 61 officers are 50 per cent out of 122. 59 professional officers is 94 per cent of the envisaged slots for professional officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would then mean that the shortage is mainly in terms of non-professional officers. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The main shortage was of professional officers. That -- you can see that in the ratio of totals in the last line. So professional officers were significantly short of the required number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if the 59 stands for -- these were the professional officers. If that is 94 per cent of the envisaged war establishment, that would mean that approximately some perhaps 64, 65, or 66 professional officers were envisaged because 59 is 94 per cent of the total. Now, if that would be true, then the shortage would mainly be with the non-professional officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know what the interpretation said, but the essence is more easily expressed like this. This percentage means that out of the total of 61 officers in the Main Staff, 59 were professional officers, which is 94 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then since you would expect 122 officers in total, then the main shortage would be in the non-professional officers. I -- I have difficulties in explaining it in any other way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The separation was not made according to whether an officer was professional or reserve, but this internal analysis was made from the viewpoint of the needs of the command, to establish the state of the cadres, professional officers, reserve officers, and total officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you explained the 61 and the 59 as referring to the professional officers and the non-professional officers. So it sounds in my ears at this moment as if you're contradicting your earlier explanation. If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know. This ratio is quite clear now. I am again saying 61 officers is the total number. 59 professional and -- I don't see the problem here. Now, up to 122, that difference can be filled with both professional or reserve officers, but there were none. So these slots, these empty slots, both professional and reserve officers were eligible for them. According to establishment, it says for a vacancy, it says "officer." It doesn't specify professional or reserve. This analysis was done for internal needs, but when you define establishment, you define a vacancy just as "officer," regardless of whether you fill it with a professional one or a reserve one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still -- I'm still a bit lost. Because there were 61 officers, if I understand you well, and earlier you told us that 59 were professional officers but I know do understand that -- well, I don't know how to understand it, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this internal analysis was made for the needs of the command. It's easiest to follow this number in the denominator, which is the total number of officers, regardless of which category. It says 61, and that's 50 per cent of the needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 61 is not the denominator; it's the numerator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My colleagues understand it, and they told me how I have to understand it, that 59 officers, professional officers as you said to us, but at least 59 out of 61, that gives a percentage of 94. I was confused because the 61 were compared to the envisaged war establishment of 122 and then that's 50 per cent. I now understand that I have to look at different columns, that 59 out of 61 is 94. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions about this table or this document, so I don't know if Your Honours had anything else that you wanted us to specifically address?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think we slowly get to understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just put one question to the witness. Can I take from this table that the Drina Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps were overstaffed at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you mean overstaffed vis-à-vis the establishment? Or in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I compare the first column with the total in the second-last column and in the last column, we see a percentage: 113 for the 1st Krajina Corps, and 115 for the Drina Corps. Can you explain these two numbers for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
