utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain each of these numbers. This percentage relates to all categories of personnel relative to establishment. So they had a bit more military personnel than envisaged by establishment. And that's the case with most armies. They have a higher complement of military personnel whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not interested in other armies. Only the two figures. That means the 1st Krajina Corps and the Drina Corps, all together, were overstaffed with respect to establishment; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had slightly more than the full complement, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ivetic, if -- at any point in time you could resolve the puzzle if the 59 officers on the first row would be 94 per cent, then it could not relate to the 61, because that would give 97 per cent. But.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've tried through the witness get the document explained. I would love to be in a position to assist you but unfortunately I'm not the one who drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness adopts this report in -- this table in his report, then at least he should be able to clearly explain what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours the Prosecution's expert is the one who adopted this table in his report and he did not explain it. That's where my confusion lies. I tried with the Prosecution expert as did Your Honour to get this explained and I don't think we got it explained. Otherwise we would still not be here asking the same questions today. To be fair to our expert, the Prosecution expert likewise was unable to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was originally drafted for internal purposes I do understand. So therefore to say that it's the Prosecution expert who failed to do what he had to do, that's -- well, we'll consider it. We consider all of your observations. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- Mr. Theunens did fully explain what this is it is at transcript pages 20526, to 20527 and that then also relates to this document, these figures, and as discussed during that testimony, the one chart that we looked at also relates to additional information that's in the report. And that's explained in the transcript. Just to refer the claim to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My problem is that when I'm logged in during the breaks I can't consult my transcripts because I'm logged in, in court. But we'll certainly look at it. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To follow up on Judge Fluegge's questions in relation to the 1st Krajina Corps and the Drina Corps, I think if I'm reading the table correctly, for the 1st Krajina Corps they had 59 per cent of the officers that were foreseen under the establishment of whom 17 per cent were professional officers; and for the Drina Corps, it looks like 45 per cent of the officers foreseen under formation of which 18 per cent were professional officers. In your opinion, what would such a figure as to officers, how would that affect command and control within the corps compared to as envisaged?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that I understand the meaning of all these numbers, and I know how they correlate. The only question is whether the ratio between them is well calculated or not. As for the 1st Krajina Corps, there were 17 per cent of officers out of the total envisaged number; and for the Drina Corps the complement was 18 per cent relative to the total existing number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the specific numbers in the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the interpreters, they've asked you to repeat since they did not get the specific numbers and please try to stress what type of officers are you talking about, since I note that that also did not get translated.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps was filled with 2.371 officers out of which 398 were professional officers. And that is 17 per cent of the total number of officers in the 1st Krajina Corps. The Drina Corps. Out of 588 officers, 108 were professional officers, and that is 18 per cent out of the total number of officers in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how would such staffing affect the abilities of the command -- of the corps to effectuate command and control as envisaged by war-time establishment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite clearly, the general conclusion is that these two commands of corps and all the operative commands shown in this table were understaffed by officers, not even one-fifth of the establishment, which adversely affected the powers, professionalism and ability to command forces in combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to shift gears, and I'd like to take a look briefly at 1D6135 in e-court. While we wait for it I can introduce it as being an outgoing code cable from Janvier, UNPF HQ, Zagreb, dated 10 August 1995 and its subject matter is memorandum of understanding with NATO and in the text it talks about air operations. I'd like to ask you about one specific section. It's on page 2. And the first paragraph says: "The provisions of this MOU relate to co-ordination between FC UNPF and CINCSOUTH concerning NATO air operations, following the NAC decisions of 25 July and 1st August 1995." And if we look down at number 4, the desired effect: "Should deterrence fail and once operations have commenced, cessation of the attack and/or elimination of the threat of attack against the Safe Area will be the desired effect. Determination of this objective having been achieved will be based upon the common judgement of CINCSOUTH and FC UNPF. In order to be in a position to make such judgement, CINCSOUTH and FC UNPF agree to share fully information on the progress and effect of the air operation and the situation on the ground." Sir, can you help out with this abbreviation CINCSOUTH. To which entity is that acronym referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The acronym and the agreement in total were adopted in terms of the following operations that occurred in the Bosnia-Herzegovina theatre of war with the activity participation of the units of the Croatian army and with the logical support of parts of NATO forces. Basically after Srebrenica and after the rapid deployment force and air force of NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, witness, sorry to interrupt, but the question was what CINCSOUTH stands for. Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of how I understand it. It means joint exchange of information and activity between the commands that signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the parties ever considered what CINCSOUTH stands for and is there any dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the Defence's position it's an acronym for particular part of the NATO alliance. I don't know if the Prosecution disputes that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I haven't really thought about it but if could I come back, I'm sure it's something that we could verify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at the item labelled number 5 and phase 1 planning, it says: "During phase 1 joint planning will be conducted to approve sets of targets to be struck, identify the zone of action ZOA," and then on the next page just briefly: "Co-ordinate modalities for air-land plans and agree on the consultive process for determining when air operations should cease." Now this document is signed by Bernard Janvier, lieutenant general, force commander of the UN Peace Forces on the one hand, and Leighton W. Smith, admiral, Commander-in-Chief allied forces, southern Europe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's CINCSOUTH.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's CINCSOUTH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the last -- page 5, I think, we'll have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- is there a page 5? I don't ... should be the page 6 in the e-court version that has that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can take into account that these are the signers of this memorandum of understanding, from a military perspective, if the UN Protection Forces are engaged in planning to identify targets to share information on the progress and effect of their operations, militarily speaking, what is the status of UN Protection Forces once they undertake these activities?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in terms of the previously presented facts in the report and especially in this period and in terms of the previous bombings, part of the UN forces openly sided with one sides in the conflict --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Ivetic please turn off his microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the planning and implementation of activities against the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska. Therefore, in this way, part of the force became a warring party.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would tender 1D06135 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there's no B/C/S translation. I think the important -- the document is of such importance that we first mark it for identification and that you take care of a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will. And I will let the translation service know that it's been requested to be done that so that it will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D06135 receives exhibit number D1356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And pending translation, it is marked for identification, under number D1356. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on Sarajevo for a bit, and I'd like to return to your report, 1D5358. 1D5358. And I'd like to turn to page 108 in the English and page 107 in the Serbian and paragraph 4.15 which in both languages bleeds over to the next page. Here, you give the demographic information for Sarajevo, and you I think refer to some of the attachments. Can you just briefly tell us what is the significance of the demographic makeup of the population? What effect did that have on the war-time situation in Sarajevo as you see it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that without being familiar with the demographic factor, its structure, and its history in this area, it is impossible to understand the beginning and the logic of the civil war in the Sarajevo theatre of war. This report establishes the direct relationship between the Sarajevo front line and the demographic structure of the town itself. Also, I think it is necessary to bring that structure into context or, rather, the context of the town municipalities. The city of Sarajevo consisted of ten municipalities. In the report and in the attachments on the basis of the census from 1991, that ethnic structure has been represented. Also, I believe that one should take into account the fact that Sarajevo was not only a Muslim city. It was also a Serb city, as a matter of fact, the biggest Serb city in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Exact numbers are provided here in terms of the structure of the entire city, how many Serbs, Muslims, Croats, Yugoslavs and other national minorities live there. The military dimension is derived from that and many other developments in the Sarajevo theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at paragraph 4.18 which is on page 111 in the English, page 109 in the Serbian, and in that paragraph, you say that the Serbs did not lay siege to Sarajevo but, rather, it was a divided city. Could you explain for us what you mean by this term "divided city"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terminology, the term "siege" is used for conflicts between peoples and states as far back as antiquity where the fate of cities was resolved in that way. "Blockade" is also a military term. Basically, this is not a blockade of the city of Sarajevo. This is a divided city and a mutual blockade of the Serb parts of town and the Muslim parts of town. There's a diagram showing the exact deployment of forces. When this is compared to the demographic structure of the city, what can be seen clearly is that throughout the war there were four municipalities with a majority Muslim population, and they were under the control of the BH army; whereas, five municipalities of the city were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. However Trnovo as, the tenth municipality of the city, changed hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 4.28 on page 112 in the Serbian and page 113 in the English, you talk about the decision of the Muslim political and military leadership not to proclaim Sarajevo a free, i.e., open, city. In a military sense, when a city is declared an open city, what obligations are on the warring sides that are imposed by international law?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Open city means that in the territory of that city there are no military forces, no military materiel. Also that there is no military action coming out of that city and also that no logistical or other support is provided to that city from another area. An open city basically means a demilitarised city. And Sarajevo, as a divided city, between the BH army and the VRS, was never an open city. It was a divided city and many of these things have been referred to in the report itself. In the Muslim part of Sarajevo, there was the General Staff of the BH army. There were all the staff units, staff support units and also independent units. At the level of the army and the majority force of a corps, which was the equivalent, if police forces are included, of 40 to 50.000 armed persons. In that context, it is impossible to speak of an open city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could just briefly take a look at 1D1255 which is an excerpt from a United Kingdom Ministry of Defence manual. I don't think we have a translation of this one so I will have to read the portion I'd like to look at. 5.38.1 which says: "The term non-defended locality has a special meaning. It is one where all the following conditions are met: "A. All combatant, as well as mobile weapons and mobile military equipment must have been evacuated; "B. No hostile use shall be made of fixed military installations or establishments; "C. No acts of hostility shall be committed by the authorities or by the population; and "D. No activities in support of military operations shall be undertaken." How does this relate to what you have been telling us in relation to what you called an open or free city?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my previously stated positions are in line with these presented here. Conclusions related to the Sarajevo theatre of war are as follows: Sarajevo was a divided, protected and mutually blockaded city. So divided, mutually blockaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender this as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to JSP 383, we see that on the facsimile header on this that it was -- it's appears to be from 2004 and the actual text of this was -- has been amended and changed. I just ask -- it's hard for me to evaluate it with respect to the amended text if I don't see the full version of the manual. Could the Defence upload that and make that available to us before we decide on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The full version? Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of whatever this comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have it marked for identification for the time being. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D01255 receives exhibit number D1357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pending -- it depends on when you receive the full copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will e-mail that, so that it gets there faster than going through the e-court system because that takes some time. And then we can upload it after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then Mr. Weber will receive it within 24 hours from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we would receive your position in the 48 hours following.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that the only thing we could possibly say is that if the particular positions here had been amended or changed, we may seek to have those amendments also admitted with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the matter we would hear from both -- at least within three days from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But I don't know what amendments after 2004 would have to do with the situation in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for whether they are there and what the observations are. Let's just proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to your report, 1D5358, and page 146 in the English and paragraph 4.137, which should be, I think, page 144 of the Serbian. I apologise, I guess it's page 146 of the Serbian and 148 of the English. 4.137. And we're almost there. Okay. And here in this paragraph, you say: "Sarajevo was a militarily occupied city, i.e., according to the terminology of the international law of war, a defended city." And in relation to this, you cite to SFRY regulations. I want to take a look at 1D456 with you, an excerpt from the Department of Army United States manual. And if we could turn to page 2 at the bottom, we see under 40, "defended place" defined: "Investment, bombardment, assault and siege have always been recognised as legitimate means of land war far. Defended places in the sense of Article 25, HR, include: "A, a fort or fortified place. "B, a city or town surrounded by detached defence positions, which is considered jointly with" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down if you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "B a city or town sir rounded by detached defence position, which is considered jointly with such defence positions as an indivisible whole. "C. Place which is occupied by a combatant military force or through which such a force is passing. The occupation of such a place by medical units alone is not sufficient to make it a defended place." And then: "Factories producing munitions and military supplies, military camps, warehouses storing munitions and military supplies, ports and railroads being used for the transportation of military supplies and other places devoted to the support of military operations or the accommodation of troops may also be attacked and bombarded, even though they are not defended." The question I have for you, General, is: How does this definition or description of "defended place" compare to what you are discussing in your report as a defended city?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is presented here are basic elements that, as a matter of fact, restrictively define the concept of a defended city. Restrictively, because they even bring into context logistical elements, namely, that such a city cannot be considered a defended city. A moment ago I presented the basic facts involved, namely, that from the very start of the civil war, even before the armies, the national or ethnic armies, were originally established, Sarajevo was being divided. There were roadblocks were being set up on both sides, and in that process of civil war, there was division. So it was a divided city and it was a defended city, on both sides. On one side, the Muslims were the majority population; on the other side, the Serb population was the majority population, and I think that this fully complies with the definition of a defended city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours we would tender this as the next document and I suppose Mr. Weber would have the same comments that he had about the UK manual so I suggest we do the same thing if that's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I can be more specific about this one. The material is incomplete, United States field army manual 2710 as it indicates by the cover page, was originally adopted in 1956. This is the appendix to the 1976 amendments. I did have an opportunity to check those and the particular provisions that were noted by the Defence have been superceded and changed so we would ask that the cover materials from this particular upload by added in to it, and we would have no objection to the admission of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we need a translation anyhow. Yes. Same. Here, there's no need to send you anything. You just check and then we'll hear from you. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D456 receives exhibit number D1358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Pending a translation, pending hearing from the Prosecution its position, the document is marked for identification under that number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about the strength of the ABiH forces in Sarajevo. I forget, you said some range beginning at 40.000 and I believe going up to some other higher number than 40.000. How significant a fighting force did this represent, the ABiH forces, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report I provided detailed information regarding the growth and reorganisation of the BH army in the Sarajevo theatre of war, especially of the 1st Corps. From the very beginning of the war, there were 38 to 40.000 troops and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we -- these details are already in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Details that have to do with the growth of the 1st Corps of the BH army, yes. That is contained in the report and there is a trend of constant growth of these forces. And that's what I wished to speak about in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just wondering whether Mr. Ivetic was asking what is already to be found in the report or whether he has any questions in addition to the report. First one is not needed. The second, of course, you could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me simplify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to other armed units of the ABiH, how did the ABiH forces in Sarajevo compare in terms of their size?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the BH army was the strongest corps of the Muslim forces throughout the war. At the end of the war, it included 78.000 persons. As for equipment and weaponry, the 1st Corps received the best weapons and equipment. And, well, I wouldn't want to go into any further detail especially ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we've got the full translation. But I think that we have enough details now for our purposes since we do have more in your report and I would like to look at some other parts of your report. So if we can return to 1D5358 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start doing that, Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you try to -- I mean, you went half an hour over your time estimate. Try to limit it to finish in the next session because that's -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do my best to move quicker and I've also been removing questions so I will aim for beating that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm especially thinking about CINCSOUTH where apparently the witness should give the answer, whereas, if you look for more than one minute at the document, everyone seems to agree on what it is. And therefore, the witness not knowing it, perhaps should not have been asked about it. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider how much time will further be granted, Mr. Ivetic. We'll do that during the break, the break which will last until 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber expects you to conclude your examination-in-chief today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, we still have a few areas to cover and we have approximately 38 minutes to finish, so if we could try to keep the answers to a -- shorter rather than longer, and if I need anything clarified, I will ask a follow-up. And I'd like to look at your report again, 1D5358, this time page 42 in the English and page 40 in the Serbian, and paragraph 4.118. And, I'm sorry, I must have misspoken, the page is 142 in the English and 140 in the Serbian and the paragraph is indeed 4.118. In this paragraph, you talk of the ABiH placing its soldiers and units amongst civilians. Is that practice in accord with military doctrine and/or law?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not in accord with either doctrine or law. That situation prevailed all the time during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 167 in the English and 165 in the Serbian, and look at paragraph 4.186. While we wait for it, in this part of the report you're examining an example of the use of artillery fire during the war as to Sarajevo and, you identify here that the artillery of Crepoljsko where the firing position of one of the corps artillery groups probably was to -- was used to neutralise the fire of enemy mortars. And the question I have is in relation to the next line that says, "The expenditure of ammunition was not even 5 per cent of the minimum required for neutralisation according to table norms." Can you please explain this concept to us. What are the table norms for neutralisation? How do they apply?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an artillery man, I know this very well. There are rules and firing tables that specify ammunition for different types of targets. They set the norms for the type of target in the specific case for -- for the calibres in question. It was determined that it was 5 per cent less than the tabled norms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, generally speaking, when artillery or mortars are used to neutralise a target, are we talking about -- what type of what number of rounds are we talking about? Are we talking about one or more?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically for this type of target, one needs five times more ammunition than indicated here, but because of the position of the target, the number of projectiles specified in the table was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to have any knowledge as to norms of ammunition expenditures for neutralisation of targets in any other armies apart from the Yugoslav ones, and how they would compare to the norms that were in place in the Yugoslav armies?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just happens so that my masters paper referred to this subject and, while writing it, I also studied foreign experiences and norms. US and Russian norms are by about 20 per cent higher than the norm in the Yugoslav People's Army and that's closely linked to the economy capacities of a given country, regardless of the fact that this process is technological.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can I ask something. You earlier said something in relation to paragraph 4.186 about tables, et cetera. The beginning of that paragraph reads that: "What was used to neutralize the fire of enemy mortars ..." Could you tell us how many mortars did the BiH army have in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the total number for the entire corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that number is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. I mean within the city of Sarajevo, that is, the -- if I could say, the inner ring I -- or the divided part of the city, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inside the city, I did not find that number, the total number for the 1st Corps, but it can be calculated indirectly through the materiel used in Sarajevo because mortars were used as battalion firing groups, and I can calculate that number arithmetically and present it the next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But how can you calculate a number? Isn't it a matter of presence of mortars which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, through the establishment of units that were within the inner ring of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But didn't you explain earlier to us that what is supposed to be there is not always there. And would that be any different from the -- for the -- for the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true, both in terms of personnel and assets of all the armies in Bosnia. The envisaged establishment was different from reality. But one can calculate a rough number within a certain range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you -- in the same paragraph I read: "The expenditure of ammunition was not even 5 per cent required for the neutralization according to table norms." But if you wouldn't know what is there on the ground, how could you then calculate that it's less than 5 per cent of the minimum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are talking about one target here. One mortar unit. That represented the battalion firing group of one battalion. Not talking about the corps. And here specifically we have one target for which there exists a norm since the JNA. It's a mortar platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in -- see if we could go in order. If we turn to page 141 in English, page 138 in Serbian, paragraph 4.111. In this part of your report, sir, you are talking about the 1994 shelling at Markale market, and in this specific paragraph, you say that one mortar shell cannot cause those casualties as seen in Markale, and you mention something about even in laboratory situations. Could you please explain for us briefly what you meant here.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the number of those killed and wounded cannot be placed in the context of one mortar projectile of 120 millimetres. Through a combination of circumstances in addition to studying the artillery capacities of individual units, I had a position in the General Staff in the technical centre of the Army of Serbia, which deals also with modelling on -- on practice grounds, and in simulating this exercise, you cannot even get approximate effects to what this projectile had, which made me conclude that it was not possible to achieve that effect with only one projectile. It had to be a reinforced explosive device with subprojectiles or shrapnel that managed to injure such a number of citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I propose to leave Sarajevo and talk about Srebrenica, which is in part 5 of your report and in 5.19 which is to be found on page 189 in English, page 187 in the Serbian, you mention the safe area agreement, the demilitarization agreement. In a military sense, is the concept of a demilitarised zone codified under law and/or doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is defined on the basis of international law and national regulations in the former JNA, and after that, the rules of active command in the Army of Republika Srpska. It is clearly defined what that area is and how it must be observed in terms of ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last few words. In terms of relation towards ... what?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're being asked to repeat last few words of your answer so the interpreters can interpret them.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in terms of norms and doctrine, it is clearly defined what that area is and how it is to be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And based upon your knowledge and review of the material, was the situation in Srebrenica following the signing of the demilitarization agreement, was it consistent with what -- did it fulfil the requirements of a demilitarised zone as understood under doctrine and law?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the enactments of the United Nations, according to reports and the documents of the BH army, according to the documents of command and reports of the VRS, as well as according to subsequent information from studies and monographs, it is obvious that that area had never been demilitarised, nor did it meet the standards of a protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In terms of the UNPROFOR forces that were put in place in Srebrenica, what is your assessment if that number of forces was sufficient to accomplish the demilitarisation of that area?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the agreement on demilitarization of that area had been observed in keeping with international law, then those forces could have been sufficient. However, since that did not happen until the end of the war and instead military forces increased from an operative group, the 8th Operative Group, to the forces of the 28th Division, the report presents information from ABH sources what the ratio of forces was, what the balance of power was, and together with the forces in Zepa, it was a 10.500 to 11.000. The conclusion is that not in a single moment since the signing of the agreement had there been any will to honour it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 5.20 which is on the bottom of our screens in both languages, you say here according to paragraph 7 of Article 60 of the Protocol and here you're talking on the Protocol of the Geneva Conventions. "If one of the parties to the conflict commits a material breach of the provisions listed above, the other party shall be released from its obligations under the agreement conferring upon the zone the status of demilitarised zone." How did this apply to the situation in Srebrenica, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's exactly as this paragraph defines it. Since there was no demilitarisation and their activities from the protected area only increased, the Army of Republika Srpska was no longer bound by the agreement because it was not a protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Moving on, if we go to page 205 in the English and 202 at the bottom of the Serbian and it bleeds onto 203, paragraph 5.69 and 5.7 [sic] of your report, you talk about the Krivaja 95 action being a forced action. Could you just briefly explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This operation, which was in a way forced upon the Army of Republika Srpska, is displayed in several ways. First, the forces of the 28th Division kept broadening the area they controlled. Ever more often and more intensively they carried out raids out of that area, committing sabotage and terrorist actions against in civilian population, and in a brief period they killed over 310 soldiers, policemen and civilians from March to June 1995. The authorities and the Army of Republika Srpska were forced, were compelled to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in terms of the operation itself, in your opinion who had operative command over the Krivaja 95 operation within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of planning and execution, it was the command of the Drina Corps based on Directive 7 and Directive 7.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we have seen footage of General Mladic on the ground in Srebrenica. How do you interpret and see the role of General Mladic on the ground during the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is natural that the commander of the Main Staff should be in the key area where combat is going on. That was typical of General Mladic throughout the war. His physical presence in some place does not mean he commands an operation, because that would also go against the regulations and the powers involved in the command over the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've had some evidence that General Mladic left Bosnia-Herzegovina for some meetings in Belgrade after the fall of Srebrenica. What effect per the military doctrine and regulations did General Mladic's departure from Bosnia to attend meetings in Belgrade have on his role as commander of the Main Staff? Could he exercise command and control when outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person - in this specific case, the commander of the Main Staff - is outside the combat zone and was not the operative commander, was instead in a neighbouring state without the technical systems and the support enabling command, it is natural that he is not commanding, he is not effectively the commander of the Main Staff and his duties are instead discharged by somebody who is on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by operation of the rules of regulations who would be that someone on the ground who commands when the commander is away?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the specific case, there was no obligation for the commander of the Main Staff to be present constantly. His second in command is the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic in this instant case, who was dealing with problems in the western part of the theatre of war, in Krajina, in the area of operation of the 1st and 2nd Corps because there was already intelligence that the Croatian army and the BH army were planning an incursion into the area of the VRS. Documents were signed by General Gvero when Mladic was absent. According to the rules, it was possible for a member of the command, the eldest officer in a certain area, to represent the Main Staff, and I believe in this case, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In which way was -- would that have been communicated to the army: The hand-over of command in the absence of the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In depth, the army is informed through a signed document. You can see from the logo, the memorandum and from the signature that a different person is signing for the given person and that you can see in the document that General Gvero signed on the 13th and 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no formal hand-over necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A formal hand-over is not necessary because it's not a hand-over of duties. It's a standing in for a certain period of absence for a superior who is absent. And that can be regulated in war situations verbally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 238 in English and it bleeds onto page 239 and page 236 in Serbian and it goes on to page 237 in Serbian, I'd like to look at paragraph 5.164.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this section of your report, and most of it is it on the next page in both languages, you are talking -- are you reciting a quotation from General Mladic at the second hotel Fontana with Mr. Nesib Mandzic and the quotation is there of the words on both pages. From a military perspective, how do you assess or understand these words?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the military point of view, I can say this, bearing in mind the nature of the army and what I said earlier, the lack of professional officers at the tactical level, and bearing in mind the previous spiral of violence and revenge in Podrinje, the victimisation of civilians in villages and populated areas around Srebrenica, I think General Mladic knew that there was a huge potential for revenge, so he insisted that arms be laid down so that the situation could be kept under control in this smaller area. And that was his main motivation in demanding that the members of the 28th Division lay down their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in relation to this same transcript of that discussion, one of the Prosecution's experts Mr. Butler said at transcript page 16831, lines 3 through 9, as follows: "I mean, in the technical sense, that Srebrenica has just been captured, General Mladic is seeking the surrender of the 28th Division rather than to continue to engage them in battle, the fact that he would offer a cease-fire and the fact that he would make the necessary provisions to allow for those individuals to travel to, in this case, the Hotel Fontana, to negotiate that surrender, I mean, that's all technically proper." Would you agree with Mr. Butler that, from a military perspective, this language is all technically proper?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as military regulations are concerned and the legality of these actions, it is all in keeping with the regulations and in keeping with the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting, General Mladic had another meeting at the Hotel Fontana and as to that meeting, first of all -- that was with other civilian leaders, including a Muslim female individual. Have you also reviewed the information as to that meeting for purposes of your review?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now with respect to the transcript from that meeting, the Prosecution at transcript page 494 through 495 has characterised that meeting as follows: "Mladic did hold a third meeting at the Hotel Fontana at 10.00 on the 12th and his murder plan began to reveal itself at that meeting." And in calling a "murder plan," the Prosecution cited to this language which I will now read to you before asking my question. The language that they considered to be the murder plan is based upon the citation, quote, of General Mladic talking to these people saying: "As I told the gentleman last night you can either survive or disappear. For your survival, I demand that all your armed men, even those who committed crimes, and many did, against our people, surrender their weapons to the VRS." 23

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a complete misstatement of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Weber is dealing with this witness. If you want to consult with Mr. Weber, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We did notify the Chamber before the witness that the Prosecution would be separating between two counsel, with Mr. McCloskey handling the Srebrenica aspect so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's not. I think it's -- it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I did know that ahead of time and I do understand that they both will be representing the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I'd forgotten about that. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I know that's not normal. It was also given the nature of the objection, the questions would have come to my direction any way so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, under those circumstances - and I must just admit that I had forgotten - if there's anything you would like to object to at this moment, Mr. McCloskey, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't object to any statement that Mr. Ivetic wants to put to the witness, but to characterise it as the Prosecution's case for the murder operation, it's just so beyond wrong that I had to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm citing from Mr. McCloskey himself in the opening statement where he describes the third meeting at the Hotel Fontana and says, "His murder plan began to reveal itself at that meeting." I don't know how else to interpret those words, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, again, "to reveal itself" means that apparently that's an element in -- that at least how I understand those words whether right or wrong, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay -- I can rephrase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apparently, you are quoting a portion of the opening statement and you'd like to put a question to the witness in relation to that quote. If you would -- do we need to repeat the quote or -- perhaps that's best and then you put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The quote is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, to simplify things, I can even ask a -- rephrase the question since the gentleman has reviewed the entirety of that third meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, do you consider any words uttered by General Mladic at that third Fontana meeting to be consistent with the Prosecution's claim that a murder plan began to reveal itself at that meeting? I think that should resolve any problems.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not learn of any murder plan in any of the materials and documents. I believe that the citation from the third conversation in Fontana is actually based on professional responsibility and the wish to protect the lives even of those who had committed misdeeds and all the others who surrendered their weapons, so that misfortune would not befall anyone, in terms of the breakout. I think that all of this was aimed at the protection of the fighters of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And we only have three more questions to go. First, I want to ask you: Are you familiar with the allegation that General Mladic, in talking with Momir Nikolic, and when asked what would happen to the Bosnian Muslim males at the soccer pitch in Nova Kasaba made a hand gesture which Nikolic interpreted as meaning that they would all be killed. We have that multiple times at our trial, including transcript page 12148 and onwards, and transcript page 11938 and onwards. My first question is, simply, are you aware of that allegation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of such allegations as I watched the footage. And that was the first time that I saw that part of the testimony. I think, and I know that in the JNA and later on in the Army of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Ivetic had three questions. The first one was whether you are aware of it. You've answered that question. Mr. Ivetic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the same, General Dannatt said that he considered such a hand gesture to be a perfectly acceptable way of conveying an order, and that's at transcript page 19052 through 19053. Do you agree with General Dannatt, that is, do you consider a professional officer can receive an order of that nature in a hand gesture that he then has to interpret?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska, according to all regulations, there was no symbolic language of issuing orders or of communication. Secondly, I think that Captain Nikolic as the security organ in a brigade and the commander of the Main Staff cannot have such communication. It is impossible. Thirdly, the organ of security to have functional relations with the commander of the Drina -- the communications person of the Drina Corps and then in terms of command with the commander of the Drina Corps, and I believe that this could not have happened this way and it could not be interpreted this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the last question: In your opinion, what obligations were by duty imposed upon Captain Nikolic if he believed that this was the way to interpret the hand gesture as an order to undertake such a drastic measure?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Functionally, he had to report to the security organ of the superior command, and in terms of the chain of command, his brigade commander. Functionally up to the top. That information would have meant unlawful action on the part of the commander of the Main Staff and measures based on the law should have then been taken vis-à-vis him. Such an order is not carried out in such a situation, and such an order would be contrary to the interests of the state and people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours as well. That completes the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Kovac, we'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just I may have missed it, but tomorrow morning, a videolink has been scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. Although I -- today I was told that that videolink may actually not last the whole day. I don't know the time estimates of both parties in relation to that. But there's a videolink scheduled for tomorrow and then for Wednesday. We had already in advance said that if the Wednesday ended early that General Kovac would return. I don't know the situation as to Tuesday, but we do need to let the general know if he will be on call for potentially part of the time tomorrow, since that was not originally communicated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the one for tomorrow the one with the two-hour direct examination estimate from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If it is, I think that that witness probably will last most of the day tomorrow and then there is a videolink also for Wednesday. So it is possible we could have a small session. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the option would be best, Witness, if you would remain at stand by, not necessarily within this building and be in touch with the Victims and Witness Section and then most likely halfway the morning, we would be able to tell you whether there's any chance that we'd like to continue your examination in the latter part of tomorrow morning's session. That would be, well, let's say, on from 12.00 or 12.30. If you would be so kind to do that, to make yourself available, though not necessarily here waiting in a small witness room. That would be appreciated. And it may well be that we'll only continue on Wednesday for you. I, again, instruct you not to speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. So, therefore, we'd like to see you back either tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you were -- touched, among other matters, also in the report in relation to -- to Markale or to the Markale incidents where the witness refers to a witness statement or testimony which he has considered which is KW586. Is that in evidence before this Chamber? Because there's no further footnoting or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is not yet in evidence. My understanding, if that's the witness I'm thinking of, that is a witness who is still on our list and may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be. I have got no idea who KW 586 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do know who it is and it is the Prosecution's understanding that the Defence will be presenting that witness so the matters might be more appropriately addressed with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, the Chamber doesn't know what the reference is about, but apparently you know, Mr. Weber, and that is, in a party-led trial, an important thing. We'll adjourn for the day, and I apologise for building to a bad reputation, not remember that tomorrow is Friday, or tomorrow is videolink day, but we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 17th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of November, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
